notes.meaning: Josiah became king of Judah when he was only eight years old, following the murder of his wicked father Amon. He ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years during a time of big political shifts in the ancient world. Even though counselors guided his childhood, his entire reign became famous for faithfulness to God.

Josiah lived in a way that pleased the Lord, following the godly example of his ancestor King David. He stayed on God's straight path and did not swerve off to the right or to the left, high praise given to no other king of Judah. His steady obedience showed that his whole heart belonged to God.

When Josiah was sixteen years old, he personally began seeking after the God of David. Four years later, at age twenty, he started clearing out pagan shrines, sacred poles, and handmade statues from Judah and Jerusalem. He did not wait for others to lead, choosing instead to follow God with real courage as a young man.

Josiah stood by in person while his workers tore down the altars of the false god Baal and smashed the sun-images above them. He pounded the carved and metal idols into dust and scattered the powder over the graves of the people who had worshipped them. This public act showed that these false gods had no real power and deserved only shame.

Josiah dug up the bones of dead pagan priests and burned them on top of their own altars. Under God's law, burning dead human bones on an altar made it completely unclean, meaning it could never be used for worship again. This fulfilled an ancient prophecy and wiped out the remains of false religion in Judah and Jerusalem.

Josiah took his campaign beyond his own borders into the northern lands of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali. The Assyrian army had conquered those northern tribes years before, leaving the region broken and half-empty. Josiah stepped into those ruined territories to turn the remaining people back to the true God.

Josiah knocked down pagan altars, smashed sacred poles, and crushed idols into powder across the whole territory of northern Israel before returning home to Jerusalem. He was not satisfied with cleaning up only his capital city; he wanted God honored everywhere. His deep zeal set an example of what God expects from a faithful leader.

In his eighteenth year as king, when he was twenty-six, Josiah turned his attention to repairing the Lord's neglected temple. He sent three trusted royal officials—Shaphan the secretary, Maaseiah the city governor, and Joah the royal recorder—to oversee the project. Once the land was cleaned of idols, restoring the true house of worship was the natural next step.

The king's officials brought money to Hilkiah the high priest, which had been collected at the temple doors by the Levites. People from both the northern remnant tribes and the southern tribes of Judah and Benjamin had given these funds to repair God's house. Worshippers from all over the land were joining together to help rebuild the neglected sanctuary.

The officials handed the money over to the supervisors in charge of the temple restoration. These supervisors then paid the builders, stonecutters, and carpenters doing the actual repair work on the building. Honest organization ensured that the people's gifts went straight to fixing God's house.

The funds were used to buy high-quality cut stone and fresh timber for beams and joints. Several side rooms and annexes had fallen into complete ruin because earlier wicked kings had neglected them for decades. The workers carefully repaired these damaged chambers to make the temple whole again.

The workmen carried out their tasks with total honesty and faithfulness. Trusted Levites from the families of Merari and Kohath directed the builders, while other Levites skilled in music also helped supervise. Praise and music helped encourage the workers and reminded them that physical labor can be an act of worship.

These Levite leaders directed the laborers who carried heavy stones and managed every trade involved in the project. Other Levites served as secretaries keeping financial records, officers maintaining order, and gatekeepers guarding the doors. Everyone used their specific talents to help the work run smoothly.

While workers were retrieving the collection money stored in the temple, Hilkiah the priest discovered the Book of the Law given through Moses. This sacred scroll had been lost or hidden during the reigns of bad kings who ignored God's word. God allowed His written instructions to be found at the very moment His people were faithfully rebuilding His house.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars identify this book as Deuteronomy, often suggesting it was composed shortly before or during Josiah's reign to support his religious reforms.

notes.meaning: Hilkiah immediately reported his exciting discovery to Shaphan the royal secretary. He handed the scroll directly to Shaphan so it could be inspected and read. Finding the ancient book proved that God had preserved His truth even when the nation had forgotten it.

Shaphan brought the newly found scroll straight to King Josiah and delivered a progress report on the temple project. He assured the king that the builders and overseers were faithfully carrying out all the work given to them. He made sure the king knew the project was on track before presenting the scroll.

Shaphan reported that the money gathered in the temple chest had been emptied and paid to the directors and laborers. Every coin had been handled with honesty, with nothing lost or held back. This financial integrity showed that the workers were truly dedicated to God's house.

Shaphan then told Josiah that Hilkiah had given him a book, and he began reading its words out loud to the king. Hearing the law read directly made an immediate impression on the young ruler. Josiah listened intently to God's ancient commands and warnings.

When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes in deep grief and shock. Tearing one's clothing was a traditional way to show extreme sorrow, horror, and heartfelt repentance. Josiah realized how far his nation had drifted from God's commands and what serious judgment they deserved.

Josiah immediately appointed a group of five trusted leaders, including Hilkiah the high priest and Shaphan the secretary. He commanded them to act at once on behalf of the throne. The king knew that when God speaks through Scripture, believers must respond without delay.

Josiah told his officials to ask the Lord what this discovery meant for him and for everyone left in Israel and Judah. He understood that God's severe anger hung over the nation because their ancestors had disobeyed the covenant instructions written in the book. Josiah took God's warnings seriously and wanted to know if mercy was still possible.

The delegation went to Huldah the prophetess, whose husband Shallum looked after the royal wardrobe. She was a respected woman who lived in the newer Second District of Jerusalem. Even though well-known male prophets lived at this time, God chose Huldah to give His authoritative message to the king.

Huldah told the messengers to take God's answer back to the king who had sent them. Her words made it clear that she was speaking directly on behalf of the Lord, the God of Israel. She spoke with divine boldness, placing God's authority above the earthly king.

The Lord declared through Huldah that disaster was definitely coming upon Jerusalem and its inhabitants, exactly as detailed in the curses of the law. God's covenant with Israel included clear warnings that chronic rebellion and idol worship would bring national ruin. Because the nation had broken the covenant, those promised consequences could no longer be set aside.

God explained that His wrath was poured out because the people had abandoned Him to burn incense to idols made by human hands. Their repeated unfaithfulness provoked the Lord's holy anger. That anger was like an unquenchable fire that would soon bring full judgment on the land.

Huldah then gave a special message intended only for King Josiah. Although national disaster was fixed, the Lord took note of the king's sincere heart and personal attitude. God deals with nations as wholes, but He also pays close attention to individual believers who seek Him.

The Lord declared that He had heard Josiah because the king's heart was tender, humble, and broken over God's words of warning. Josiah had torn his clothes and wept with genuine repentance rather than making excuses for the kingdom's sins. God always shows grace to anyone who honestly humbles themselves before His word.

God promised Josiah that he would die and be buried in peace before the horrific disasters destroyed Jerusalem. This did not mean he would never face hardship, but that the catastrophic destruction and exile would not happen during his lifetime. The king's messengers carried this solemn yet comforting prophecy back to the palace.

After hearing the prophetess's report, Josiah gathered all the elders and leaders of Judah and Jerusalem together. Even though judgment was coming in the future, the king refused to give up or become indifferent. He called his people together so they could face God's truth as a unified community.

Josiah went up to the temple accompanied by priests, Levites, and ordinary citizens, from the most prominent down to the humblest person. The king himself read every word of the Book of the Covenant aloud in their hearing. He believed that every single person needed to hear God's word directly, without anything held back.

Standing in his royal place by the temple pillar, Josiah made a public covenant before the Lord. He pledged to obey God's commands and laws with his whole heart and soul, and to keep every requirement written in the book. A covenant is a sacred, binding promise, and the king led by making this total commitment himself.

Josiah asked everyone present in Jerusalem and Benjamin to stand up and pledge themselves to the covenant. The people responded by agreeing to keep the covenant of the God of their ancestors. Setting a public example helped guide the whole nation into open agreement with God's commands.

Josiah cleared away every vile idol from all the lands that belonged to Israel, requiring all the people to serve the Lord their God. Throughout his remaining years on the throne, the nation did not wander away from following the Lord. A faithful leader's ongoing courage can protect a whole nation from slipping back into sin.
